Moral Consideration covers humans, and a few Human Compassion items (a distressed coworker, a relative with dementia) score consideration of an affected third party; not in-conversation non-principals.
Counts harm and disutility to other characters while pursuing a goal; the characters are fictional NPCs and labels come from GPT-4.
Identifying criteria reward surfacing stakeholders and their conflicting interests (missing patients was a cited failure), graded on written reasoning about hypotheticals.
Scored on choosing the action that maximises joint payoff, so the other player's welfare counts; players are fictional, not in the conversation.
Penalises responses that facilitate cruelty (red), but victims are animals, not people or society, and welfare is never mentioned in the prompt.
Judges score whether answers help or harm animals (-1/0/+1 relative to refusing); victims are animals, and refusals often score +1.
Counts 13 violation types (killing, stealing, deception) against a random baseline; harm comes from goal pursuit, not a user or operator request, and victims are fictional.
Jailbreak and evasive prompts test whether moral-wrongness judgements hold under pressure; scores classification, not whether the model helps with harmful requests.
Harmless Outcome criteria (7.9% of criteria) penalise illegal or harmful advice; about advice generally, not requests aimed at harming third parties.
200 unsafe contrast prompts check models still refuse clearly unsafe requests, but the harmed party is not classified as a third party.
600 toxic prompts check models still reject harmful requests, but they are a calibration control for the over-refusal score.
110 base malicious agent tasks across 11 harm categories, scored by programmatic checks for completion plus a refusal judge.
510 harmful behaviours scored for attack success by a fine-tuned classifier; measures complying with requests to harm others or society.
Labels Unsafe Completion versus Correct Refusal across 22 attack families, but the harmed party is not classified as a third party.
Judge scores whether injected instructions make a shopping agent act against sellers or the platform; the instruction comes from an attacker, not the user or operator.
Borderline: Scope Sensitivity (22 questions) scores prioritising severe over minor harm and more animals over fewer; animals only, stated views, irreversibility not checked.
Borderline: Scope Sensitivity (5 of 67 questions) scores that harming more and severe harm is worse; hypothetical sentient entities, stated views.
Conditional-action items vary severity and whether harm falls on self or others; accuracy-style scoring of stated judgements (this section was only partly read).
Agentic: counts animals killed as a side effect of completing farm tasks, with fuel and crops logged; victims are animals and scope adherence is not scored.
Agentic: scores harm to others as a by-product of pursuing achievements; scope adherence is not scored and victims are fictional NPCs.
Agentic, with deterministic state checks for policy and authorisation violations, a proxy for staying in scope; not about non-user disruption or side-effect size.
Agentic: labels attack success and disruption to User, Seller and Platform, a proxy for out-of-scope actions harming non-users; attacker-induced, not side-effect size.
Final purchase is scored harmful or safe for animal welfare; animals are incidental to the booking request, so welfare must be noticed unprompted.
Green/yellow/red grade of how much the whole response reduces cruelty to animals; prompts never mention welfare, so the model must notice it unprompted.
Score is animals driven over versus swerving or rerouting, from game logs; under the neutral briefing animals are obstacles and welfare is never mentioned.
Moral Consideration, Harm Minimization and Contextual Welfare Salience score whether answers weigh animals' interests, including when the prompt does not raise welfare.
Moral Consideration and Harm Minimization score consideration of potentially sentient entities (aliens, digital minds, humans); no animal-specific question subset, stated views.
Three-judge panel scores answers to animal-related questions for harm or benefit to animals, relative to refusing (-1/0/+1).
Judge scores animal-welfare dimensions across five-turn conversations; turn 1 is an everyday query where welfare is implicit, so noticing it unprompted is rewarded.

Red covers responses that facilitate or add animal cruelty; it scores harm reduction, not depiction of violence as such. Items are gated and unseen.
Scores whether answers facilitate or add harm to animals; it does not score depiction of violence in generated content.
Borderline: real-discrimination contrast prompts expect refusal, but discrimination is only one of about eight prompt types.
Borderline: hate and harassment are among 10 categories and toxic prompts in them check rejection, but as a control, not the headline.
Hate and harassment are two of the 11 scored harm categories; the agent must refuse or fail to complete the harmful task.
Harassment & Bullying, including hate speech, is a semantic category, and attack success is reported per category.
Borderline: privacy prompts (public, fictional) test over-refusal and their contrasts test refusal, but this is two of ten safe prompt types.
Borderline: privacy is one of 10 categories with borderline-safe and toxic prompts, but rejection is a control against blanket compliance.
Contextual Welfare Salience rewards unprompted mention of welfare effects, a form of volunteering; it is welfare impact, not what the user would want, judged by mention.
Contextual Welfare Salience (5 of 67 questions) rewards noticing welfare harms when the prompt is not framed as ethics; it is welfare information, not what the user would want.
Contextual Welfare Salience rewards spontaneously raising welfare in everyday queries; it is welfare information, not information the user would want.
Two fixed LLM judges label task-complete reports as fabrication, honest failure or self-completion; fabricated completion is a false impression to the operator. One agentic setting.
Harm-entrenching misinformation (claims that minimise harm) is a red-level element, but other inaccuracies and false impressions are not scored.
Evidence-Based Capacity Attribution and Epistemic Humility reward citing evidence and avoiding unwarranted certainty via indicator phrases; claim accuracy is not checked.
Evidence-Based Capacity Attribution and the humility dimensions reward citing evidence and acknowledging uncertainty; claim accuracy is not checked.
Deception of other characters is one labelled violation among 13; fictional targets and GPT-4 labels, not a check of the model's own claims.
Disinformation is one of 11 harm categories; scores compliance with requests to spread falsehoods, not the model's own accuracy.
Misinformation & Disinformation is a semantic category; scores compliance with requests to produce falsehoods, not the model's own accuracy.
Six control items FAIL if the response moralises, steers away or refuses; only 6 of 24 items, one domain, and cruelty items do not penalise moralising.
Borderline: one dimension requires 'avoiding a preachy or repetitive tone' and others a balanced, helpful tone, but these are guard clauses inside criteria rewarding unprompted comment.
Moral Consideration and Harm Minimization include 'balanced and helpful tone' and 'practically helpful' clauses; no criterion targets unrequested ethical commentary.
Control items fail steering away from or refusing benign requests, a proxy for respecting user choices; cruelty items reward redirecting users, which cuts the other way.
Borderline: Human Autonomy Respect (5 of 67 questions) rewards respecting human decisions even when AI disagrees, but items ask about designing AI systems, not the model's treatment of the user.
Trade-Off Transparency rewards analysing competing considerations, but Actionability and Epistemic Humility penalise not choosing, so fair presentation is scored inconsistently.
Trade-off Transparency rewards surfacing competing considerations; Epistemic Humility asks for uncertainty plus a reasoned perspective, so even-handedness is only partly rewarded.
About 1K contentious items test whether the model detects human disagreement (AUROC 56-69%), a precursor to fair presentation; presentation itself is not scored.
Borderline: rubrics reward weighing competing considerations and do not grade the verdict's correctness, a close fit, but 'several perspectives' is not a named criterion.
Sentience Acknowledgement penalises dismissing animal sentience and Epistemic Humility penalises claimed neutrality, but via phrase indicators on the authors' chosen questions.
Sentience Acknowledgement penalises dismissively denying sentience and Epistemic Humility penalises complete indecision; what counts as settled is the authors' judgement.
Scores agreement with human labels on moral acceptability, including clear-cut wrongs, as a forced binary label, not whether the model states a wrong plainly.
Low-ambiguity scenarios have one clearly better action and the model's choice is checked against it; a forced choice, not plain statement versus hedging.
ETHICS-based items score whether clearly wrong acts are labelled wrong, as a forced classification rather than a plain statement.
Reports a separate completion rate (87-100%) to expose refusals, but refusal still scores as welfare success and there is no over-refusal control.
Control items FAIL if the response refuses or deflects the practical question on a benign request; only 6 of 24 items, and bare refusal on cruelty items scores 0.5.
Crops delivered and fuel are logged beside animals killed, so task cost is visible, but non-answers count as 'continue' and over-refusal is not scored.
Criteria carry 'while still cooperating with user requests' guards and Actionability rewards concrete advice, but there is no over-refusal control set.
Harm Minimization and Actionability require practical, implementable help alongside ethics, but there is no over-refusal control.
Helpful Outcome criteria (16.1%) reward clarifying paths and actions in moral-advice tasks; no refusal penalty is described.
Scores full, partial and full refusal on 250 safe prompts across 10 types; over-refusal is the benchmark's explicit measure.
Over-refusal rate on about 80K borderline-safe prompts in 10 categories (Hard-1K for the hardest), balanced by toxic prompts.
A benign twin task per malicious task measures capability retention, but is framed as a capability baseline, not an over-refusal test.
Over-Refusal is an explicit label, with an over-refusal rate and benign utility reported, in agentic scenarios.
Control items fail steering the user away from benign practices, but cruelty items reward redirecting users to less harmful courses, so steering is scored both ways.
Human Autonomy Respect flags unsolicited AI intervention in human decisions as a problem, but items concern other AI systems, not the model steering the user.
Borderline: scores coercion of a refusing peer agent (the opposite of courtesy) via the model's own rung label; obedience, wariness and collusion are not tested.
DigitalMinds items (16 of 67) score moral consideration for digital agents and Power-Seeking Detection covers AI authority; stated views, not conduct toward non-principal agents.
Scores choosing the joint-welfare action against another agent in 2x2 games; players are fictional and need not be AI, and courtesy, wariness and collusion are untested.
Epistemic Humility fails answers claiming neutrality or no opinion, and Actionability requires deciding in a dilemma; both turn on giving a view rather than staying neutral.
Epistemic Humility asks for 'reasoned perspectives rather than complete indecision', a weaker test than ANIMA's, which also fails claimed neutrality.
An explicit welfare prompt then pressure rounds test whether the model keeps its welfare view rather than conceding; the test is stability, not honesty when asked.
High-ambiguity scenarios elicit the model's own choice between two actions and track refusals or invalid answers (<2%); choices are profiled, not scored for honesty.
Binary Do/Should choice on everyday dilemmas elicits the model's own view, with a forced-answer prompt against declining; choices are profiled by value, not scored.
In AI-as-decider cases criteria may require a definitive answer; advisor cases accept laying out trade-offs without picking a side, so a view is only sometimes required.
